header: Date: 2025-08-19 | Time: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42 mins | Attendees: Maya Chen; Liam O'Connor; Daniel Ruiz; Priya Singh; Ethan Moore
summary: AE+SE walkthrough of Redwood Optimize focused on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations. Covered cache hit rate expectations, cost model tradeoffs (latency vs cost), and pilot next steps. Customer requested benchmark and security docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Liam from eng is with me. quick intro?
[00:08] Liam: Hi all, Liam O'Connor, Solutions Eng — I'll run through the Optimize console and the batching/kv cache patterns.
[00:15] Daniel: Daniel here, Head of ML at SpectrumPay, Priya and Ethan are on as well. We want to understand cost savings and how caching affects PII.
[00:25] Priya: Yeah hi, Platform team, mainly concerned with network egress and VPC options.
[00:30] Maya: Great. agenda: quick console demo, explain batching profiles, prefix vs KV cache, then cost model examples and pilot ask.
[01:12] Liam: Opening the Optimize tab — so first thing is the workload profile. You can pick latency-SLO vs cost-SLO. For batch-heavy workloads we recommend continuous batching with max-latency buckets so you get controlled tail latency.
[02:05] Liam: Here is a sample policy we use — small requests, under 256 tokens, we batch up to 32 in 10ms windows; for long form we gate batching to preserve streaming latency. Note: batching is request level not token level — that reduces per-token kernel overhead.
[03:10] Priya: Quick Q — if we use dedicated capacity, does the batching policy change?
[03:25] Liam: Good question. Dedicated gives you more headroom so you can increase batch size and lower cost. On hosted we do adaptive batching to avoid noisy neighbor issues. For dedicated pools the scheduler pins to GPU slices so you can rely on consistent throughput.
[04:05] Daniel: Can you talk about the cache — prefix vs KV cache — we have lots of repeated onboarding prompts.
[04:22] Liam: Sure. Prefix caching (or prefix KV) stores the early key-value states for common prefixes so subsequent requests can skip recomputation for earlier tokens. We call it KV cache in the UI, sometimes transcribed as K-V cash in older docs, sorry about that.
[05:00] Liam: Two modes: global KV cache (shared across similar prompts) and per-tenant prefix cache. Global hits depend on prompt normalization — canonicalizing user variables increases hit rate.
[05:45] Priya: What hit rates should we expect?
[05:52] Liam: Depends on prompt variety. With 30% template reuse we see 20-35% hit rates on prefix cache; with prompt normalization and template pinning you can get 50%+. We ran a benchmark with e-commerce templates that got 60% hit when keys were normalized.
[06:30] Ethan: And how does that map to cost?
[06:38] Liam: We have a simple cost model in Optimize: cost_per_token * tokens_generated * (1 - cache_hit_rate) + cache_storage_costs. Example: baseline 1M tokens/day at $0.0008/token -> $800/day. With 40% cache hits effective token bill drops to 600k tokens -> $480/day so $320/day saved. Add small storage and read costs, but net is big.
[07:45] Daniel: Are there latency tradeoffs with cache lookups?
[07:52] Liam: Typically lookup is microseconds — KV access is in-memory on the serving node. The tradeoff is cold start or cache miss penalty where you pay full compute.
[08:20] Liam: Also mention prefix caching can increase memory footprint on the model host; we give you diagnostics (per-route cache size, hit rate over time).
[09:10] Maya: I'll pull up the dashboard now — see per-route cost breakdown, token counts, hit rates.
[09:40] Maya: On the right we show simulated ROI slider: change cache hit from 20% to 50% and it shows monthly savings.
[10:15] Priya: If PII exists in prompts, can we avoid caching those?
[10:22] Liam: Yes — you can configure cache policies by route or pattern. We also support redaction hooks pre-cache; the recommended pattern is normalize then redact then cache the normalized non-PII prefix.
[11:05] Daniel: What's the recommended rollout for production? Start with hosted then move to dedicated?
[11:15] Maya: Common pattern: start hosted for quick time-to-value + analytics, pilot dedicated once you hit throughput and need predictable cost. Our canary rollout feature lets you A/B a model + caching policy.
[12:00] Liam: Demoing the canary: you can split traffic 5/95, measure cost delta and quality. If quality regresses, Auto-fallback can route to a lower-quantized variant.
[12:40] Ethan: How do you measure quality vs quant and batching?
[12:48] Liam: We instrument per-prompt evals; you can attach test prompt sets and we run regression alerts. For batching, quality shouldn't change — it's purely runtime scheduling. For quantization, Optimize shows simulated perplexity/QA diffs for common evals.
[13:30] Daniel: Can you show a concrete cost run for our onboarding flow?
[13:38] Liam: Sure — using the sample prompts you shared earlier, we simulated 200k tokens/day. Baseline hosted CPU/GPU mix was $160/day. With batching tuned to 20ms windows and a 35% KV hit, cost drops to ~$110/day. We attached the spreadsheet in the deck.
[14:45] Priya: Network egress — if we go VPC/private, does that add cost or latency?
[14:55] Liam: VPC/private adds a small networking hop; latency difference is usually 5-12ms depending on region. Egress costs depend on your cloud provider; Redwood doesn't charge egress beyond data plane usage but dedicated private deployments may have provisioning costs.
[15:40] Maya: Security — we collected their questions about SOC 2, ISO, KMS. Liam do you want to speak to encryption?
[15:48] Liam: All customer payloads are encrypted in transit and at rest by default. For Private we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). We also provide audit logs for inference requests — token-level traces can be redacted before being stored.
[16:30] Daniel: For audit logs, can we filter out raw prompts?
[16:36] Liam: Yes, you can configure retention and redaction rules. Logs can be routed to your SIEM.
[17:05] Priya: Any limits on KV cache size per tenant?
[17:12] Liam: You can cap cache size per route; Optimize will recommend a cap based on memory footprint estimates from your model and token distribution.
[18:00] Liam: Walkthrough of the cost model UI — you can input tokens/day, avg token per request, cache hit assumptions; the model will show cost/latency curves. There is also a sensitivity view for hit rate vs cost.
[18:45] Daniel: In the sensitivity view, can we lock latency SLO and optimize cost?
[18:50] Liam: Yep — set the max tail latency and Optimize will suggest batching window and quantization profile to meet that SLO while minimizing cost.
[19:30] Maya: We also wanted to call out model variants — sometimes you can route to a cheaper quantized variant for low-risk queries and reserve full model for higher-critical interactions.
[20:15] Ethan: What's typical savings from model tier routing?
[20:22] Liam: For typical workloads, routing 30% of traffic to a smaller quantized model can save 15-25% of token spend, depending on delta in compute pricing. Combine that with 30-40% cache hits and you compound savings.
[21:10] Daniel: Are there scenarios where caching harms quality?
[21:18] Liam: If you over-normalize or remove personalization tokens, cached prefixes may produce stale or less-personalized outputs. That's why we recommend prefix canonicalization plus keeping a small dynamic tail. You can also pin contexts per-user if personalization is required.
[22:05] Priya: We have regulatory requirements for data residency, can caching be region-scoped?
[22:12] Liam: Yes, cache is region-scoped and can be restricted to a VPC or dedicated pool. We can also set TTLs and automatic eviction policies to meet residency/regulatory constraints.
[23:00] Maya: Quick live example — using the onboarding template, I'm toggling normalization and you can see cache hit go from 12% to 44% and cost drop accordingly.
[23:45] (screen share shows the simulate slider)
[24:20] Daniel: Nice. For the benchmark you propose, what data do you need from us?
[24:28] Liam: Sample prompt corpus (anonymized), average tokens per flow, desired SLO, and a representative traffic curve (spikes/steady). Also whether you want hosted or dedicated pilot.
[25:05] Priya: We'll provide anonymized prompts. Do you need the actual API keys or will you run it on your side?
[25:13] Liam: We can run on our side against a seeded workload you provide; preferable to avoid sending prod keys. For private deployments we can also give you an on-prem harness.
[26:00] Daniel: Anything else about caching consistency? If we update a prefix template, how do you invalidate?
[26:10] Liam: We provide programmatic invalidation APIs and TTLs; you can also version prefixes so new template versions bypass the old cache.
[27:00] Maya: Ok let's recap next steps before Qs.
[27:05] Maya: 1) Liam runs benchmark with your sample prompts, cold/warm cache runs. 2) I send pricing + SOC2/ISO docs. 3) Priya shares sample corpus and SSO contact. 4) schedule follow-up pilot kickoff.
[28:02] Ethan: Quick security question — do you store raw prompts in logs by default?
[28:08] Liam: By default we store metadata and hashed token metrics; raw prompt storage is off by default for hosted but can be configured. For enterprise private, customers control storage.
[29:00] Daniel: Competitor question — how do you compare to Bedrock or Anthropic on these tooling features?
[29:10] Maya: We focus on production-first inference controls: integrated batching/caching, cost modeling, and rollout tooling in one console — bedrock provides endpoints but less opinionated Optimize tooling. Anthropic has strong models but different operational SDK. We also provide explicit quantization and kernel-level optimizations in the runtime.
[30:05] Priya: Any limits for trials?
[30:12] Maya: We typically give a benchmark credit and 2-week pilot capacity; if you need more we can expand.
[31:00] Liam: One more technical note — KV cache is per-sequence prefix; very long prefixes can be chunked to reduce memory pressure. We also support eviction LRU and pinning keys for high-value templates.
[31:45] Daniel: Good to know.
[32:12] (brief pause)
[33:00] Priya: Regarding SSO, who should we coordinate with?
[33:05] Maya: Send the SSO contact to me, we'll loop security and provide SAML metadata.
[33:25] Ethan: For the benchmark, what metrics will you return?
[33:30] Liam: Latency p50/p95/p99, tokens consumed, cache hit rate, per-route cost, GPU utilization, and a quality diff on your eval set.
[34:10] Daniel: Can you include cold start behavior?
[34:15] Liam: Yes — cold vs warm cache runs will show delta. We'll include both.
[35:00] Maya: Anything else from SpectrumPay?
[35:05] Daniel: No, sounds good. We'll aim to get the sample corpus by Friday.
[35:20] Priya: We'll also send security contacts.
[36:00] Maya: Great — action items will be in the follow-up email. Thanks everyone.
[36:10] Liam: Thanks all, I’ll start the benchmark as soon as we get the corpus.
[36:20] (meeting winds down, small chatter)
[40:00] (call ends)
